detail.extracted_title: The Shore of Dates and Water: Five Hundred Kilometers Across 1763 Oman (Part II)
detail.excerpt: In Part I of this three-part historical series, dense summer monsoon fog drove the Dutch East India Company ship Amstelveen onto the volcanic reefs of Ras Madrakah before dawn on August 7, 1763. Seventy-five men were lost in the surf, leaving third mate Cornelis Eyks and twenty-nine barefoot castaways stranded five hundred kilometers south of Muscat.
detail.article_html:
Cornelis Eyks knew that staying near the wreckage meant death. As the August sun climbed over the Arabian Sea, the black volcanic cliffs of Ras Madrakah turned into an oven. Nothing edible had washed ashore from the shattered hull—the ship's heavy cargo of Javanese sugar had dissolved into foaming brine within minutes of impact. With no shoes, no freshwater canteens, no charts, and no firearms, the thirty survivors turned their backs on the surf and began walking north along the edge of the sea.

Barefoot Across Bar Al Hikman

The first days tested what the human body could endure. Wearing little more than salt-stiffened rags, the castaways picked their way barefoot across scorching gravel plains, jagged limestone ridges, and beds of razor-sharp coastal shells. Blisters rose, burst, and packed with fine sand. Within forty-eight hours, their tongues had swollen from dehydration. Whenever a dry wadi cut toward the beach, men dropped to their knees and clawed shallow pits into the gravel hoping to reach trapped rainwater, only to hit bitter brine.

North of the cliffs, the coastline flattened into the blinding, sun-cracked salt pans of Bar Al Hikman. Sheets of mirage water shimmered across the white horizon while the ground radiated relentless heat. One by one, weakened sailors collapsed from sunstroke and exhaustion. Comrades tried supporting those who stumbled, but their own strength was rapidly giving out.

In the small journal he guarded throughout the march, Eyks recorded each loss with spare, heavy brevity. Eight men died along that desolate stretch of coast, their bodies laid beneath quiet cairns of stone beside the Arabian Sea. Twenty-two men walked on.

First Contact Opposite Masirah Island

Near the southern edge of the sands opposite Masirah Island, the survivors spotted movement along the dunes—a band of local Bedouin camel herders and coastal fishermen working the shore.

The first moments were taut with uncertainty. Neither group shared a single word of language, and the ragged Europeans were unrecognizable strangers washed out of the monsoon haze. Warily inspecting the castaways, the herders stripped the few remaining pewter buttons and metal belt buckles from their torn breeches.

Yet no hand was raised in violence. As soon as the Omani fishermen looked closely at the men's cracked lips, bleeding feet, and hollow eyes, caution gave way to an older coastal law: a traveler dying of thirst on the shore is a guest under protection.

Dates, Well Water, and the Road to Sur

Leading the twenty-two Dutchmen to a wind-sheltered cluster of palm-frond huts (arish), the villagers drew cool, sweet water from a deep stone-lined well. Knowing that gulping water too fast could cramp a starving stomach, they handed each sailor small, measured sips first. Then woven palm mats were unrolled in the shade, and wooden bowls were set down between the strangers: heaps of soft dates (tamr) and fresh coastal fish fried in oil over driftwood fires. For men who had survived for days by prying raw shellfish off wet rocks, that quiet meal marked the boundary between death and life.

Across the weeks that followed, that same code carried the castaways up Oman's eastern seaboard from one small fishing settlement to the next. People whose own livelihoods depended on scarce wells and seasonal catches gave what they had without hesitation. Villagers tore strips of spare cloth so the sailors could bind their cut feet against hot stone. Families shared dried sardines and dates for the road ahead. Whenever tidal inlets or treacherous salt flats blocked the coast, local elders sent guides to walk beside the foreigners until they reached the next inhabited outpost safely.

Passing through Al Ashkharah and rounding the easternmost shoulder of the Arabian Peninsula at Ras Al Hadd—where the heavy monsoon rollers of the Arabian Sea yield to the calmer waters of the Sea of Oman—the twenty-two survivors finally sighted the busy wooden shipyards and whitewashed houses of Sur after five weeks on foot. Their desert march was over; ahead lay a coastal dhow to Old Muscat and a forgotten logbook that would wait two centuries to be rediscovered.

Sources

  • Cornelis Eyks, Noodlottige Gevallen van het Volk van 't Schip Amstelveen (1766)
  • Klaas Doornbos, Shipwreck and Survival in Oman, 1763 (translated into Arabic by Fatima Salim Al Ajmi in collaboration with the Ministry of Heritage and Culture)
detail.instagram_caption:
After the Dutch East India Company ship Amstelveen shattered on the submerged volcanic reefs of Ras Madrakah before dawn on August 7, 1763, third mate Cornelis Eyks and twenty-nine barefoot survivors faced five hundred kilometers of dry coastline between their gravel beach and Muscat.

In Part II of our three-part historical series, the thirty castaways turn north across scorching limestone ridges and the blinding salt pans of Bar Al Hikman. Digging into dry wadi gravel yielded only bitter brine, and eight companions perished from heat exhaustion along the shore before the remaining twenty-two men encountered Bedouin camel herders and coastal fishermen opposite Masirah Island.

What followed preserved twenty-two foreign lives. Led into palm-frond coastal shelters, the starving sailors were given measured sips of cool stone-well water, wooden bowls of soft tamr dates, fried fish, cloth strips to bind their bleeding feet, and local guides who walked them safely past tidal flats through Al Ashkharah and Ras Al Hadd into Sur.

Read Part II of the Amstelveen survival account at omanspire.om (link in bio).
